subject: Archaeology
title: Uruk: The World's First Megacity
description: One-minute skill: Uruk: The World's First Megacity.

hook.text: By 3100 BCE, Uruk in southern Iraq had 40,000 residents — the largest city on earth and the birthplace of writing.

buildup.text: Uruk had monumental temples, city walls, craft workshops, and a canal system linking it to the Euphrates River.

discovery.text: The earliest known written tablets were found here — simple pictures pressed into clay to track grain and livestock.

twist.text: The legendary King Gilgamesh is said to have built Uruk's walls.

climax.text: Uruk's influence spread across the ancient world. Colonies with Uruk-style pottery appeared from Turkey to Iran.

punchline.text: The world's first city invented writing to count sheep. Literature came later.

quiz.question: What were the earliest written tablets at Uruk used for?
options: Recording prayers and hymns to the gods
Tracking grain and livestock with simple pictures pressed into clay
Writing letters between kings of neighboring cities

details.summary: Uruk in southern Iraq was the world's first true megacity, home to perhaps 80,000 people by 3000 BCE. It pioneered monumental architecture, bureaucratic administration, mass production of goods, and — most significantly — the invention of writing.
details.whyItMatters: Uruk represents the moment human settlements crossed the threshold into urban complexity. Its innovations in writing, administration, and architecture became the template for civilizations that followed.
takeaways: Uruk housed up to 80,000 people by 3000 BCE
Writing was invented here around 3200 BCE for record-keeping
It pioneered monumental architecture and bureaucratic administration

faq.question: How do we know Uruk was so large?
faq.answer: Archaeological surveys mapped the city walls enclosing over 5.5 square kilometers. Pottery and settlement density within those walls, combined with estimates from comparable ancient cities, suggest a population of 40,000 to 80,000 at its peak.

faq.question: What was writing first used for in Uruk?
faq.answer: Not poetry or religion — accounting. The earliest clay tablets record quantities of grain, livestock, and goods. Writing began as a bureaucratic tool to manage surplus and trade in a city too large for oral memory alone.
